scenario_stem:
Ferncombe Cheese Co is a family-run cheese maker founded 9 years ago in a rural valley in Country X. It employs 14 staff and produces 60 tonnes of handmade cheese a year. Around 70% of output is sold through Marlowe Wholesale Foods, a national wholesaler that charges an 18% margin and supplies 45 independent shops, while the farm shop sells the remaining 30% at $14 per kg. The wholesaler pays $9 per kg.

Annual revenue last year was $630,000. Marlowe Wholesale Foods has offered to buy an extra 15 tonnes a year if Ferncombe invests $90,000 in a new maturing room, using up all spare winter capacity. Alternatively, Ferncombe could spend $45,000 expanding its farm shop and expect to sell 4 more tonnes each year at $14 per kg.

questions.question_text: Define 'wholesaler'.
questions.model_answer: A wholesaler is a business that buys goods in large quantities from producers and sells smaller quantities to retailers or other businesses [2].

knowledge_max_2: buys goods in large quantities/bulk from producers
sells in smaller quantities to retailers or other businesses

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ferncombe Cheese Co of selling through Marlowe Wholesale Foods.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Marlowe Wholesale Foods buys in bulk, so Ferncombe can sell large volumes of its 60 tonnes a year without visiting every shop itself [k], reaching 45 independent shops in one commercial deal rather than 45 separate ones [app]. Benefit 2: A wholesaler holds stock and breaks bulk close to the 45 independent shops [k], giving Ferncombe a steady outlet that helped it earn $630,000 in annual revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: buys in bulk, allowing the producer to sell large volumes without many separate visits
holds stock and breaks bulk, providing a convenient and steady outlet
application_max_2: reaching 45 independent shops through one deal
helping earn $630,000 annual revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Ferncombe Cheese Co of relying on Marlowe Wholesale Foods.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Marlowe charges an 18% margin, so Ferncombe receives only $9 per kg from wholesale sales instead of $14 per kg at the farm shop [k], cutting the revenue earned on the 70% of output sold through the wholesaler [app], which leaves less profit available to invest in the maturing room or farm shop expansion [an]. Problem 2: Relying on one wholesaler gives Marlowe strong bargaining power over a small producer [k], so its offer of an extra 15 tonnes a year could tie up all spare capacity in a low-margin channel [app], weakening Ferncombe's independence and pricing power over time [an].

knowledge_max_2: the wholesaler takes a margin, so the producer receives a lower price per unit
reliance on a single buyer gives that buyer bargaining power over a small producer
application_max_2: 18% margin means Ferncombe gets $9 per kg instead of $14 per kg
70% of output goes wholesale; the extra 15 tonnes offer would tie up spare winter capacity
analysis_max_2: less profit per kg reduces funds available for reinvestment
dependence on one buyer weakens independence and long-term pricing power

questions.question_text: Do you think Ferncombe Cheese Co should accept the wholesaler's offer of an extra 15 tonnes a year? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting would secure a reliable bulk buyer for an extra 15 tonnes a year [k]. At $9 per kg this is about $135,000 a year of extra revenue (15,000 kg x $9), using spare winter capacity that would otherwise go unused [app], and it would strengthen the relationship with Marlowe, encouraging them to keep Ferncombe in the 45 independent shops [an]. However, the offer requires $90,000 for a new maturing room and commits the extra output to the wholesale channel at just $9 per kg, far below the $14 per kg paid at the farm shop [k]. Expanding the farm shop for $45,000 could sell 4 more tonnes at $14 per kg, about $56,000 a year, for half the investment [app], though accepting both options is impossible while winter capacity is tight [an]. Overall, Ferncombe should accept the offer, because $135,000 of secure extra revenue outweighs the sacrificed direct sales if the firm can finance the maturing room without strain [eval], but it should keep at least part of output for the higher-margin farm shop to preserve direct customer relationships [eval].

knowledge_max_2: accepting secures a reliable bulk buyer for extra volume
however, it locks spare capacity into a lower-margin channel and requires heavy new investment
application_max_2: 15 tonnes at $9 per kg gives about $135,000 a year (15,000 kg x $9)
farm shop alternative: $45,000 for 4 tonnes at $14 per kg, about $56,000 a year; maturing room costs $90,000
analysis_max_2: accepting strengthens the wholesaler relationship and uses spare capacity, lifting revenue
however, lower margin per kg, commitment of limited capacity and investment risk reduce flexibility
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation weighing $135,000 revenue gain against $90,000 outlay and lower margins
overall judgement that balances short-term revenue against independence and channel mix

scenario_stem:
Brightwick Candles is a small business in Country X making scented soy candles in a home workshop. Founded 3 years ago, it employs 6 staff and makes about 8,000 candles a month. Sales last year reached $240,000, with 75% of revenue coming from three regional distributors supplying 12 gift shops and 25% from weekend craft fairs.

The owner is considering an e-commerce website costing $15,000 to build and $400 a month to run, expecting online sales of $60,000 in the first year. Demand is highest at Christmas, so the workshop currently turns away seasonal orders. However, she worries about postage costs eating profits on single candles, online payment fraud and customers not trusting a brand they cannot smell first. She could instead spend $6,000 on extra craft fair pitches.

questions.question_text: Define 'channel of distribution'.
questions.model_answer: The route taken by goods or services from the producer to the final consumer, which may involve intermediaries such as wholesalers and retailers or may be direct [2].

knowledge_max_2: the route goods take from producer to consumer
may involve intermediaries or be direct to the consumer

questions.question_text: Explain two ways e-commerce could benefit Brightwick Candles.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: An e-commerce website would let Brightwick sell its candles directly to consumers across the country, beyond the 12 gift shops supplied through its distributors [k], so the expected $60,000 of first-year online sales would add a new revenue stream on top of the $240,000 earned last year [app]. Benefit 2: Selling online means the shop is open 24 hours a day at a running cost of only $400 a month [k], so Brightwick can take orders outside craft fair weekends without paying for extra pitches [app].

knowledge_max_2: e-commerce widens market reach beyond existing physical outlets
online sales are open continuously at low running cost
application_max_2: expected $60,000 first-year online sales would add to last year's $240,000
reaching beyond the 12 gift shops at $400 a month running cost

questions.question_text: Explain two problems e-commerce could cause Brightwick Candles.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Customers cannot smell soy candles before buying online [k], so some orders, especially for the $60,000 first-year target, could end in disappointment, returns and refund costs, while postage on single candles would eat the margin [app], eroding profit on small orders [an]. Problem 2: E-commerce exposes the business to online payment fraud and cyber-security risks [k], so Brightwick must pay for secure payment processing plus $400 a month hosting on top of the $15,000 build cost [app], diverting cash from the $6,000 extra craft fair pitches it could alternatively secure [an].

knowledge_max_2: customers cannot inspect/test the product before buying online
payment fraud and cyber-security risks are inherent to e-commerce
application_max_2: postage on single candles eats the margin; first-year online target is $60,000
$15,000 build cost plus $400 a month hosting, compared with spending $6,000 on craft fairs
analysis_max_2: returns and refund handling erode profit on small online orders
extra security and hosting costs drain cash that could be used for proven fair sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Brightwick Candles should launch its own e-commerce website? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Launching the website would widen Brightwick's market beyond the 12 gift shops and weekend craft fairs it already uses [k]. If online sales reach the expected $60,000 in the first year, they would add about a quarter to last year's $240,000 revenue [app], while the 24-hour shopfront keeps selling when fairs are closed, helping a 3-year-old business grow quickly [an]. However, the website costs $15,000 plus $400 a month to run, and customers cannot smell soy candles before buying [k]; fraud, postage on single candles and refund handling could erode the thin margins Brightwick makes on weekend fair sales [app]. At the same time, $6,000 on extra craft fair pitches would grow the channel that already delivers 25% of revenue [an]. Overall, Brightwick should launch the website, because $60,000 of new annual revenue outweighs the setup cost if it prices delivery sensibly and takes secure payments [eval], but it should keep the craft fairs as a face-to-face showcase and review the website's return on investment after 12 months [eval].

knowledge_max_2: owning a website widens market reach beyond existing physical channels
however, setup and running costs plus inability to inspect goods online are risks
application_max_2: expected $60,000 first-year online sales versus $240,000 revenue last year
$15,000 build cost, $400 a month running cost, $6,000 alternative craft fair spend
analysis_max_2: 24-hour shopfront supports fast growth beyond fair weekends
fraud, postage and refunds could erode margins; fair channel is proven and cheap to expand
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation weighing $60,000 extra revenue against $15,000 plus running costs
overall judgement recommending launch with delivery priced sensibly and a 12-month review

scenario_stem:
Solmara Herbal Teas is a private limited company in Country X blending organic herbal teas from locally grown herbs. Founded 6 years ago, it employs 20 staff and produces 90 tonnes a year. Exports to Country Y account for $520,000 of annual revenue, sold through a single distributor that stocks 40 shops but has cut prices by 12%.

A speciality food agent has offered to represent Solmara in Country Y, promising introductions to 150 speciality shops in return for 8% commission on sales. Buyers at two recent trade fairs requested free samples, and Country Y retailers praised the light leafy flavours. Alternatively, Solmara could open its own sales office in Country Y, costing $85,000 a year plus travel, keeping full control of pricing, promotion and branding.

questions.question_text: Define 'agent'.
questions.model_answer: A person or firm that acts on behalf of a business to arrange sales in a market, earning a commission but not taking ownership of the goods [2].

knowledge_max_2: acts on behalf of another business to arrange sales

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Solmara Herbal Teas of appointing an agent in Country Y.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The agent already knows the Country Y food trade and speciality food retailers [k], so Solmara could reach 150 speciality shops instead of the 40 stocked by its current distributor [app]. Benefit 2: The agent is paid only a commission on actual sales [k], so Solmara pays 8% of sales rather than committing $85,000 a year plus travel to its own office [app].

knowledge_max_2: an agent has local market knowledge and buyer relationships
an agent costs only commission, so no fixed cost is incurred before sales are made
application_max_2: access to 150 speciality shops instead of the 40 currently stocked

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Solmara Herbal Teas of opening its own sales office in Country Y.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: An own office gives Solmara full control over pricing, promotion and branding in Country Y [k], so it could stop the 12% price cuts and hold prices steady across the 150 target shops [app], protecting its premium image and margins on the 90 tonnes it produces a year [an]. Benefit 2: A permanent office builds direct relationships with retailers and gives fast response to market changes [k], so Solmara can gather feedback and launch new herbal blends quickly [app], strengthening retailer loyalty and long-term export sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: own office gives full control over pricing, promotion and branding
a permanent office enables direct retailer relationships and fast feedback
application_max_2: reversing the 12% price cuts across 150 target speciality shops
responding quickly for the 90 tonnes of annual production with locally gathered feedback
analysis_max_2: price control protects premium image and margins
direct relationships build loyalty and sustain long-term export sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Solmara Herbal Teas should appoint the agent in Country Y? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Appointing the agent would cost only 8% commission on actual sales [k], which on $520,000 of annual exports is about $41,600 a year, far less than the $85,000 office cost plus travel [app], and would immediately open doors to 150 speciality shops, triple the 40 shops currently served [an]. However, an agent is not an employee, so Solmara would keep less control over how its tea is presented and priced [k]; the 12% price cutting could continue if the agent chases volume, and Solmara's brand could be weakened in Country Y [app], which may reduce its ability to charge premium prices later [an]. scenario_stem:
Brancott Catering Co is a private limited company providing mobile event catering for weddings and corporate parties in Country X. Founded 4 years ago, it employs 8 staff and generated $322,000 last year from 46 events, with an average value of $7,000 per event. Word of mouth supplies most bookings.

A hotel group in the capital has offered to refer wedding clients in return for a 12% fee on every referred booking. Most enquiries arrive by phone or social media message, and summer Saturdays fill up 6 months ahead. Alternatively, Brancott could spend $7,500 on its own website with online booking, targeting corporate clients directly; the owner expects 2 extra events a month worth about $7,000 each, while venue referrals might add 15 events a year but at lower margins.

questions.question_text: Define 'e-commerce'.
questions.model_answer: Buying and selling goods or services over the internet, for example through a website, app or online booking platform [2].

knowledge_max_2: buying and selling goods or services over the internet
carried out through a website, app or online platform

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why selling services directly to customers suits a service business such as Brancott Catering Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Services are intangible and cannot be stored or transported, so they are normally sold direct from provider to customer [k], matching how Brancott already wins most of its 46 events through word of mouth [app]. Reason 2: Selling direct lets Brancott meet clients personally to plan each event [k], so each $7,000 event can be tailored to the customer's menu, budget and schedule [app].

knowledge_max_2: services are intangible and cannot be stocked, so direct selling is typical
direct sale enables personal consultation and tailoring of the service
application_max_2: most of Brancott's 46 events already come through word of mouth

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks for Brancott Catering Co of relying on hotel-group referrals.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: The hotel group would take a 12% fee on every referred booking [k], so on 15 referred events a year at $7,000 each Brancott would pay about $12,600 in fees, cutting the margin left for ingredients and staff [app], weakening profit per event over time [an]. Drawback 2: Referred clients are effectively loyal to the hotel rather than to Brancott [k], so if the hotel ends the partnership or switches caterer, Brancott could lose those 15 events a year without owning the customer relationships [app], making future revenue less predictable [an].

knowledge_max_2: an intermediary takes a fee that reduces the producer's margin per sale
reliance on a referral partner creates dependency and weakens the producer's direct customer relationships
application_max_2: 12% of 15 referred events at $7,000 each is about $12,600 a year
loss of referred clients if the hotel switches caterer or ends the deal
analysis_max_2: fees directly reduce profit retained per event
dependency makes revenue unpredictable and weakens Brancott's bargaining position

questions.question_text: Do you think Brancott Catering Co should rely on referrals from the hotel group? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Relying on the hotel group would bring about 15 extra events a year worth roughly $105,000 at $7,000 each, with almost no marketing effort from Brancott [k]. Even after paying the 12% fee of about $12,600 a year, the referred bookings would add useful volume while Brancott builds its pipeline [app], and hotel clients could introduce Brancott to premium wedding customers it could not reach alone [an]. However, the 12% fee would recur every year, costing far more than a one-off $7,500 website plus modest hosting [k], while the owner expects 2 extra corporate events a month from the website at about $7,000 each, roughly $168,000 a year with no commission taken [app]. Owning that channel gives Brancott customer data, direct repeat bookings and full margin [an]. Overall, Brancott should not rely on hotel referrals as its main channel; it should invest in the website and accept hotel referrals only as a short-term top-up while online enquiries build [eval], because owning its own marketing channel protects margins and customer relationships in the long run [eval].

knowledge_max_2: hotel referrals deliver predictable extra volume with little marketing effort
however, the recurring fee exceeds a one-off investment in an own website
application_max_2: 15 referred events x $7,000 = about $105,000 a year, fee about $12,600 a year
website expected 2 extra events a month at $7,000 = about $168,000 a year, no commission
analysis_max_2: referrals can add volume quickly and access premium wedding clients
own website builds customer data, direct repeat bookings and full margin

scenario_stem:
Torncliffe Kayak Co is a private limited company making touring kayaks in Country X. Founded 11 years ago, it employs 28 staff and builds about 850 kayaks a year, selling them at an average price of $1,150. Revenue last year was $977,500, with 80% of sales through 22 independent watersports retailers and the rest at the factory showroom.

Each kayak is built by hand in under 3 weeks and carries a 5-year hull guarantee. The directors want to sell more kayaks online. A national online marketplace would charge 15% commission on each sale and already receives 2 million visits a month. Alternatively, Torncliffe could build its own website for $30,000, plus about $90 per kayak for delivery and packaging, keeping the full selling price but having to attract customers itself.

questions.question_text: Define 'direct to consumer'.
questions.model_answer: Selling goods or services straight to the final customer without intermediaries such as wholesalers or retailers, for example through a factory shop or website [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits Torncliffe Kayak Co could gain from selling kayaks directly to consumers online.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Selling direct removes the retail margin built into the 80% of sales currently made through 22 independent watersports retailers [k], so Torncliffe keeps the full $1,150 average price per kayak rather than the lower trade price [app]. Benefit 2: A direct online channel reaches paddlers nationwide who never visit a watersports shop [k], expanding the market beyond the 850 kayaks a year currently built [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Torncliffe Kayak Co might face selling through an online marketplace.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The marketplace charges 15% commission on each sale [k], so on a $1,150 kayak each sale would cost Torncliffe about $172.50, far more than the $90 delivery and packaging for its own website [app], leaving a lower margin per boat and less profit to reinvest [an]. Problem 2: Marketplace listings appear side by side with rival brands, encouraging price comparison [k], so Torncliffe may have to discount its touring kayaks to win sales [app], eroding the premium brand image built over 11 years [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Torncliffe Kayak Co should sell through the national online marketplace rather than its own website? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The marketplace already receives 2 million visits a month [k], giving Torncliffe instant access to a huge paddling audience without first spending $30,000 on its own website [app]. For a firm building about 850 kayaks a year, even a modest conversion rate could lift online volume while Torncliffe learns which models sell best without upfront promotion spend [an]. However, the 15% commission costs about $172.50 per $1,150 kayak, almost double the $90 delivery for own-site orders, and the marketplace owns the customer data and shopping experience [k]. A Torncliffe website would keep the full margin, let it retarget accessory sales and control its branding, but it would take time and ongoing promotion to attract visitors [app]; over hundreds of sales the commission bill would quickly dwarf the $30,000 build cost [an]. Overall, Torncliffe should start with the marketplace only as a 12-month trial to build awareness [eval], then shift sales to its own website once enough online orders cover the $30,000 build cost, which at about $172.50 saved per kayak needs only around 174 online sales [eval].

scenario_stem:
Fernbrook Press is a private limited company producing organic fruit juices in Country X. Founded 5 years ago, it employs 12 staff and presses 30,000 litres a month. It sells mainly through 60 independent shops supplied by one wholesaler, with revenue last year of $480,000.

In January, Fernbrook launched a subscription website offering 4 weekly deliveries at $18 per box, costing $12,000 to set up. The wholesaler takes 14 days to pay invoices, squeezing cash flow each month, and spring is the busiest season. After 4 months, subscriptions reached 300 households, but 3% of boxes arrived damaged and some subscribers cannot taste the juice before buying. The wholesaler has just offered to extend coverage to 65 shops if Fernbrook guarantees weekly deliveries.

questions.question_text: Define 'retailer'.
questions.model_answer: A business that sells goods in small quantities directly to consumers, usually from a shop or other consumer-facing premises [2].

knowledge_max_2: sells goods in small quantities directly to consumers

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Fernbrook Press of selling juice directly to consumers through its subscription website.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A subscription gives Fernbrook a predictable, recurring revenue stream [k], with 300 households signed up in 4 months each paying for 4 weekly deliveries at $18 per box [app]. Benefit 2: Selling direct removes the wholesaler's margin and the retailer's mark-up [k], so Fernbrook keeps more of the $18 box price and can reach health-conscious households nationwide beyond the 60 independent shops it supplies now [app].

knowledge_max_2: subscriptions provide predictable recurring revenue
selling direct keeps more of the selling price by removing intermediary margins

questions.question_text: Explain two threats that buying juice on a subscription website poses to consumers.
questions.model_answer: Threat 1: Online buyers cannot taste or inspect juice before paying [k], so they risk buying flavours they do not enjoy, unlike in the 60 independent shops where they can sample first [app], which can cause disappointment or wasted boxes [an]. Threat 2: Delivery can fail or arrive damaged [k], as shown by the 3% of subscription boxes that arrived damaged [app], so consumers pay for juice they cannot use and may face refund delays and inconvenience [an].

knowledge_max_2: online shoppers cannot inspect or test products before buying
delivery problems can damage goods before they reach the customer

questions.question_text: Do you think Fernbrook Press should prioritise its subscription website over extending wholesale shop coverage? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The subscription website could transform Fernbrook from a supplier dependent on one wholesaler into a brand with direct customer relationships [k]. The 300 households signed up in 4 months already generate recurring revenue, and the $12,000 setup is modest against $480,000 of annual revenue [app]. Direct sales also give Fernbrook data on flavours and delivery timing to plan the 30,000 litres it presses each month [an]. However, e-commerce brings real threats for consumers and for the business: 3% of boxes arrived damaged and buyers cannot taste first [k], which can drive refunds, complaints and bad reviews [app], while the wholesaler's offer to extend coverage to 65 shops would secure immediate in-store volume in 5 more shops with tasting that builds trust [an]. scenario_stem:

questions.question_text: Do you think Rusthaven Engineering Ltd should replace the agent with its own sales representative? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Rowanhill Knitwear is a private limited company designing and knitting wool sweaters and cardigans in Country X. Founded 8 years ago, it employs 40 staff and sells through 80 independent clothes shops and 2 department stores. Revenue last year was $2.4 million.

Half of revenue comes from sweaters and cardigans sold in autumn and winter, so stock must be ready by September. The directors must choose a route to grow sales. They could launch their own online shop at a cost of $40,000, with packaging and postage adding about $6 per garment, or they could sign a deal with Haversham Wholesale, which would place Rowanhill Knitwear in 120 shops but demand a 20% discount on trade prices. Online trials suggest 5% of parcels would come back as returns, and customers cannot try garments before buying.

questions.question_text: Define 'distribution'.
questions.model_answer: The process of getting goods from the producer to the final customer, including transport, storage and the channels used, such as wholesalers, retailers or direct sales [2].

includes transport, storage and the channels of distribution used

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Rowanhill Knitwear might face if it launches its own online shop.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Customers cannot try sweaters and cardigans before buying [k], so the expected 5% return rate would add postage, repackaging and refund costs on top of the $40,000 setup [app]. Problem 2: Knitwear is seasonal and visual, so Rowanhill must keep improving photography and website content to compete online [k], adding ongoing spending beyond the $6 per garment packaging and postage [app].

online fashion needs continuous website and photography investment

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits Rowanhill Knitwear would gain by signing with Haversham Wholesale.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Haversham Wholesale would place Rowanhill Knitwear in 120 shops, 50% more than the 80 independent clothes shops it supplies now [k], quickly growing sales volume and total revenue beyond $2.4 million [app], strengthening its market position before rivals react [an]. Benefit 2: Haversham manages ordering, warehousing and delivery to shops [k], taking over logistics so Rowanhill's 40 staff can focus on design and knitting [app], lowering strain on the business while the 2 department store relationships continue [an].

knowledge_max_2: a wholesaler places the brand in far more shops, growing volume and revenue
a wholesaler handles ordering, storage and delivery to retailers

40 staff freed to focus on design while 2 department stores still hold the range
analysis_max_2: wider distribution grows volume faster than internal sales effort could
outsourced logistics reduces operational strain and supports continuity

questions.question_text: Do you think Rowanhill Knitwear should sign with Haversham Wholesale rather than launch its own online shop? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Signing with Haversham Wholesale would instantly widen distribution from 80 to 120 shops, so sales could rise well beyond $2.4 million without the $40,000 website build or the 5% return headache [k]. The wholesaler handles logistics and reorders, letting Rowanhill focus on design, and shop stock is financed by Haversham rather than Rowanhill [app], spreading risk and supporting faster national coverage [an]. However, Haversham demands a 20% discount on trade prices, so Rowanhill would earn less per garment and remain dependent on one intermediary for growing shop distribution [k]; the online shop would keep full price and customer data, with $6 packaging per parcel, though 5% returns and no try-on would deter some buyers [app], and online traffic and trust take years to build [an]. Overall, Rowanhill should sign with Haversham now, because immediate volume into 120 shops beats waiting for online traction [eval], but it should renegotiate the 20% discount after 12 months of results and start building its online presence once cash flow improves [eval].

scenario_stem:
Saltpan Lobster Co is a family fishing business in Country X, founded 7 years ago, employing 8 fishermen on 2 boats. It lands about 30 tonnes of live lobsters a year. Around 80% are sold to a wholesale fish market at $14 per kg and 20% go directly to 12 local restaurants at $22 per kg. Revenue last year was $468,000.

The owners could spend $25,000 on a refrigerated van to deliver live lobsters to 20 more restaurants each week. The 2 boats fish 5 days a week, weather permitting, and landings peak in July and August. However, lobsters sold wholesale need no marketing or extra staff, payments arrive reliably, and the wholesale market currently takes every lobster the boats land.

questions.question_text: Define 'intermediary'.
questions.model_answer: An independent business that helps move goods from producer to consumer, for example wholesalers, retailers or agents, earning a margin or commission for its role [2].

knowledge_max_2: an independent business between producer and consumer
includes wholesalers, retailers or agents, earning a margin or commission

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why selling lobsters directly to restaurants suits a perishable product such as live lobsters.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Live lobsters are perishable, so every hour of transit matters [k], meaning short direct trips to the 12 local restaurants keep them fresher than a longer journey through the wholesale fish market [app]. Reason 2: Selling direct removes intermediary handling and margins [k], so Saltpan can charge $22 per kg instead of $14 per kg, keeping an extra $8 per kg on every lobster sold direct [app].

knowledge_max_2: perishable goods need the shortest possible channel to stay fresh
selling direct avoids the intermediary's margin or mark-up
application_max_2: short direct trips to 12 local restaurants keep lobsters fresher than the wholesale route
$22 per kg direct versus $14 per kg wholesale, an extra $8 per kg

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why wholesale markets remain important to fishing businesses such as Saltpan Lobster Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The wholesale fish market takes the full catch whatever the volume [k], giving Saltpan a guaranteed outlet for the 24 tonnes a year that currently go through it [app], securing reliable weekly cash flow without finding 32 individual direct buyers [an]. Reason 2: Selling wholesale needs no van, extra staff or marketing [k], avoiding the $25,000 refrigerated van and the daily effort of chasing $22-per-kg restaurant orders [app], keeping overheads low and letting the 8 fishermen focus on fishing [an].

wholesale sales require no extra vehicle, staff or marketing spend

avoids the $25,000 refrigerated van and daily management of restaurant orders
analysis_max_2: guaranteed outlet secures consistent revenue and working capital
lower overheads let the business concentrate on fishing rather than distribution

questions.question_text: Do you think Saltpan Lobster Co should buy the refrigerated van and sell more lobsters directly to restaurants? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying the van would let Saltpan supply 20 more restaurants directly at $22 per kg [k]; shifting 6 tonnes a year from the wholesale rate to the direct rate would add about $48,000 of revenue (6,000 kg x $8 extra per kg) without catching more lobster [app]. Fresher deliveries would also build restaurant loyalty and justify premium menu pricing [an]. However, the van costs $25,000 and brings fuel, insurance and maintenance costs, and the direct channel only works if 20 restaurants order reliably every week [k]; dropped or forgotten orders would leave perishable stock worthless [app], and the wholesale market still guarantees an outlet for any unsold catch and pays reliably [an]. Overall, Saltpan should buy the van, because moving more volume to the $22-per-kg direct channel clearly beats $14 per kg for a freshness-critical product [eval], but only after the 20 restaurants commit to standing weekly orders, with the wholesale market kept as a fallback for unsold stock [eval].

if restaurants cancel or volumes vary, perishable stock is lost and the van becomes a fixed burden

balanced judgement retaining the wholesale market as an outlet for unsold stock

scenario_stem:
Tidemill Electrical is a private limited company running 2 independent electrical goods shops in country towns in Country X. Founded 15 years ago, it employs 26 staff. Revenue last year was $1.8 million, but sales have fallen 12% over 2 years as online discounters undercut its prices.

The directors could build a website with click-and-collect for $35,000 plus $1,500 a month to maintain, letting customers order online and collect in store. It stocks about 1,400 product lines from 3 national suppliers. An online rival sells a $700 television for $549. The alternative is to remain a specialist high street retailer: 70% of Tidemill's customers say expert advice and free installation of kitchen appliances are why they shop there, and installation earns $300,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'click-and-collect'.
questions.model_answer: A service where a customer orders goods online and collects them in person from a shop or depot at a chosen time [2].

knowledge_max_2: order placed online, typically paid for in advance
goods collected in person from a shop or depot

questions.question_text: Explain two threats e-commerce poses to Tidemill Electrical.
questions.model_answer: Threat 1: Online discounters carry lower store overheads and can undercut high street prices [k], as the rival selling a $700 television for $549 shows, helping drive Tidemill's 12% sales fall over 2 years [app]. Threat 2: Customers who buy online skip the shop entirely [k], so Tidemill loses walk-in trade that supports its $300,000 a year of kitchen appliance installation business [app].

knowledge_max_2: online discounters can undercut physical shops because they have lower overheads
online buying removes the store visit, cutting walk-in trade for physical retailers
application_max_2: a $700 television sold online for $549 undercuts Tidemill's pricing
the 12% sales fall over 2 years and the $300,000 installation income both reflect store traffic

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits Tidemill Electrical could gain from a click-and-collect website.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Click-and-collect lets Tidemill sell online while still driving customers into its two country-town shops [k], protecting footfall and upselling the kitchen appliance installation that already earns $300,000 a year [app], defending revenue and margins [an]. Benefit 2: Click-and-collect removes home delivery costs and waiting times [k], making online buying attractive for heavy items such as televisions and washing machines at a running cost of only $1,500 a month [app], improving convenience and customer loyalty [an].

knowledge_max_2: click-and-collect combines online ordering with in-store collection
click-and-collect avoids home delivery costs and delays
application_max_2: in-store collection drives upselling of the $300,000 a year installation service
$1,500 a month running cost for heavy items such as televisions and washing machines
analysis_max_2: store visits protect add-on sales and margins that pure delivery would lose
convenience versus home delivery can win back price-checking customers and build loyalty

questions.question_text: Do you think Tidemill Electrical should invest in a click-and-collect website? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing in click-and-collect would let Tidemill compete online while keeping its two shops relevant [k]; at $35,000 build cost and $1,500 a month running cost, it is cheaper than losing 12% of a $1.8 million business, about $216,000 of revenue at risk [app], and it converts browsing into store visits where advice and installation can be sold [an]. However, Tidemill cannot match online prices such as $549 for a $700 television, so price-led buyers may still leave [k]; the website only works if stock is visible online and collection is easy, and at $18,000 a year running cost the system must win back meaningful volume [app], otherwise the investment becomes an expensive brochure [an]. Overall, Tidemill should invest, prioritising click-and-collect over price cuts because its differentiator, advice and installation valued by 70% of customers, cannot be copied by online rivals [eval], and it should review sales versus the $216,000 at risk after 12 months [eval].

however, the firm cannot match online discounters on price alone
application_max_2: $35,000 setup plus $1,500 a month ($18,000 a year) versus about $216,000 revenue at risk from a 12% fall on $1.8 million
the $549 rival television example shows price competition is unwinnable; advice and installation valued by 70% of customers is the firm's edge
analysis_max_2: click-and-collect protects footfall and installation upselling worth $300,000 a year
execution risk: poor stock visibility or collection experience would make it an expensive brochure
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to invest in click-and-collect rather than cut prices
balanced judgement requiring a 12-month review against the $216,000 revenue at risk
